sentences.text: He went alone at thirteen and he did it on purpose and there is no version of the story in which he did not know exactly what he was doing.

It was the second week of June, which in that part of Sweden means the light does not go, and he told his sister he was walking to the ridge and he took a phone and a bottle of water and he went to the big spruce with the buckled rings.
He wanted to see 1904 from the inside and find out what had happened.
That was the whole ambition and he thinks now that it was a reasonable one.

There is a hundred and twenty-first ring in that tree that goes wrong on one side, and Nils had a theory involving a windthrow in the neighbouring stand, and he had worked out that if he could see the buckling properly he could tell which direction it had come from.
His sister found him at twenty past four in the afternoon.
She was sixteen and had not wanted to come out and had spent the walk composing what she was going to say to him.

She had come out at about three because he had not answered his phone and had not come back for lunch, and it took her the best part of an hour to find the tree, and when she got there he was standing with his forehead against the bark and his hand flat on the trunk beside him and he did not respond to his name the first two times.
He had been there since half past nine in the morning.
He was not hurt.
He was not cold, in June.
He had drunk none of the water.
He had, by his own account, been looking for something in the region of ten minutes, and had been about to stop.
His sister did not tell their parents and Nils has never known whether that was the right call.

What she did was hit him, once, hard, on the arm, which he has always thought was fair, and then sit down on the moss and cry for a while, which he had not expected at all and which is the part he thinks about.
He sat down next to her and did not say anything useful.

He was thirteen and had nothing available except *I'm fine*, which he said about four times and which was true and which was not the point, and it took him until roughly his twenties to work out what the point had been.
She had walked into a clearing and found her brother standing against a tree not answering to his name.
Whatever was or was not happening inside that spruce, what she had was fifteen seconds of not knowing, and nothing that happened afterwards took those back.
He is thirty-one.
He works in the forest, which surprises nobody.
He does thinnings and windthrow clearance and he has taken down perhaps eleven thousand trees, which he does not find difficult and which people always expect him to.

He looks perhaps four times a year and he has never gone alone again, and the arrangement is now his sister, who lives in Umeå and who drives up for it, and who has never once suggested that they stop.
He never did work out 1904.

He can see the buckling perfectly well and it is the direction he expected, and there is a hundred and twenty-first ring in a living spruce on a ridge in Västerbotten that has an answer in it and does not have a question, and Nils has come to think that this is true of most of what is in there.
